newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha rejects Albanian opposition call.
newsitem.headline: Berisha rejects Albanian opposition call.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Tuesday rejected an opposition call for a broad-based government to end the country's bloody unrest and said he was "unshaken" in his determination to uphold law and order.

In a statement read out in his name on state television, Berisha accused the Socialist Party of organising "armed rebellion" in the south of the Balkan state, where parliament has declared a nationwide state of emergency.
"You decided to overturn the constitutional order and Albanian democracy through an armed rebellion and created a grave problem for the country," the statement said.

It was issued after Socialist leaders said they had met Berisha and called on him to end the emergency measures and establish a broad-based government to help end the crisis rocking Europe's poorest state.

"I cannot go beyond my competence. It is not up to me to decide which party or parties are going to make up a coalition. I am against a coalition between the Democratic Party and the Socialist Party, Berisha said.
Berisha was re-elected to a second five-year term on Monday by parliament, where his Democrats hold virtually all the seats.
He said he had been ready to withdraw but the opposition had taken his offer as a sign of weakness. "You responded with the organisation of armed rebellion," he said.

The ballot went ahead a day after the parliament declared an immediate state of emergency and gave security forces orders to shoot on sight at armed rioters in several towns in the south, including the port of Vlore and the coastal town of Sarande.
More than 20 people have been reported killed in the region since Friday after protesters stormed police and army weapons depot and went on a rampage of looting and burning.
The Socialists deny Berisha's allegations that they have orchestrated the unrest, born from the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes, in an effort to grab power.
"We advised him that we would never want power through blood," Pandeli Majko, one of the leaders who met Berisha on Tuesday, said.
Berisha said the emergency measures should have "very limited consequences" for civil rights and confirmed that tight media control would not affect foreign news organisation.
But he said his priority was to restore the rule of law. "I would like to make clear to you...my unshaken determination to ensure complete respect for constitutional law," he said
The Socialists, successors to the communists who ruled Albania with a Stalinist iron fist until 1990, are the biggest force in an 11-party opposition Forum for Democracy.
"We told Berisha we were ready for a wide political accord under which he would stop using the army...and we would agree to form a new broad-based government," Majko told Reuters.
"We are convinced it will be difficult to achieve this but we told Berisha it is no longer a matter of left or right but of protecting people and stopping further blood from being shed."
